concepts.concept: Magical Number Seven Plus or Minus Two
concepts.definition: Miller's foundational observation (1956) that immediate memory span for randomly ordered, meaningful items (chunks) is approximately 7±2 items, establishing the first quantified upper bound on working memory capacity via absolute judgment and span-of-attention tasks.
key_refs: Miller 1956 / The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information
Psychological Review 63(2):81-97
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's simultaneous visible control count must respect the ~7-item baseline, though modern research (Cowan) shows effective practical limit is lower when task-dependent strategies are controlled.

concepts.definition: Nelson Cowan's revised capacity limit (2010) distinguishing between task-dependent span (influenced by rehearsal and grouping strategies) and fundamental central storage capacity, which holds only 3–5 meaningful items in young adults under boundary conditions that prevent processing strategies.
key_refs: Cowan 2010 / The Magical Mystery Four: How is Working Memory Capacity Limited, and Why?
Current Directions in Psychological Science 19(1):51-57
concepts.implication: The 3–5 item core limit is the critical hard constraint for MetroGraph UI: visible simultaneous controls, nodes, or information items should rarely exceed this threshold without progressive disclosure or external offloading.

concepts.definition: Cognitive strategy of grouping multiple discrete items into larger meaningful units (chunks) to increase apparent working memory capacity; effective span depends on prior knowledge and the ability to organize information into familiar patterns.
key_refs: Miller 1956 / The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two
Cowan 2010 / The Magical Mystery Four
concepts.implication: MetroGraph can increase effective capacity through domain-specific visual chunking (e.g., grouped nodes, semantic clustering) but must not rely on chunking alone to exceed the 3–5 core limit under novel or high-cognitive-load conditions.

concepts.definition: Baddeley & Hitch's foundational 1974 model positing working memory consists of a central executive controlling task management, a phonological loop for verbal information, a visuospatial sketchpad for visual-spatial information, and (later) an episodic buffer for integrated representations.
key_refs: Baddeley & Hitch 1974 / Working Memory Model
Hitch, Allen & Baddeley 2025 / The Multicomponent Model of Working Memory Fifty Years On, Quarterly Journal of Experimental Psychology
concepts.implication: MetroGraph, as a visual system, primarily engages the visuospatial sketchpad; design must respect that both visual and verbal processing compete for the central executive, and multimodal presentations (graph + text + annotations) can create interference.

concepts.definition: Sweller's framework distinguishing intrinsic load (inherent task difficulty), extraneous load (poorly designed instruction/interface), and germane load (task-supporting cognitive effort); establishes that learning and task performance cannot exceed working memory capacity.
key_refs: Sweller 2005 / Cognitive Load Theory of Multimedia Learning, Cambridge Handbook chapter
Sweller, van Merriënboer & Paas 1998 / Cognitive Architecture and Instructional Design, Educational Psychology Review
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must minimize extraneous load (UI clutter, poor information architecture) and maximize germane load (task-aligned visualizations), recognizing that total load cannot exceed the fundamental 3–5 core capacity in novel tasks.

concepts.definition: Temporal attention bottleneck (~500ms duration) where the second of two rapidly presented targets (RSVP paradigm) cannot be reported; arises from working memory encoding bottleneck and demonstrates hard capacity limits under task interference conditions.
key_refs: Raymond, Shapiro & Arnell 1992 / Temporary Suppression of Visual Processing in an RSVP Task
Fischler et al. 2012 / Functional Imaging Reveals Working Memory and Attention Interact to Produce the Attentional Blink, fMRI evidence
concepts.implication: Rapid sequential information changes in MetroGraph (e.g., fast node transitions, rapid query results) risk triggering attentional blink; design should pace information revelation to allow working memory consolidation (~500ms minimum inter-event intervals).

concepts.definition: Concurrent visual working memory tasks interfere at the storage stage when combined set size exceeds capacity; encoding and retrieval processes are minimally affected, indicating the bottleneck is in maintenance of simultaneous items.
key_refs: Woodman, Vogel & Luck 2012 / Drag-to-select but not click-to-select creates similarity-based interference in working memory, Journal of Neuroscience
Morey & Cowan 2005 / When visual and verbal memories compete
related_concepts: Encoding vs. Storage vs. Retrieval Stages
concepts.implication: MetroGraph interactions that require simultaneous visual attention to multiple elements (e.g., comparing node attributes, tracking edge relationships while filtering) can exceed capacity and fail; sequential or progressive disclosure patterns are necessary.

concepts.definition: Lavie's framework showing that task-irrelevant distractors are processed only when perceptual load is low and spare capacity remains unused; high perceptual load consumes available resources, reducing distraction but increasing load.
key_refs: Lavie 2005 / Load Theory of Selective Attention and Cognitive Control, Psychological Review
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must carefully balance perceptual load: too many simultaneous visual elements consume attention (high load, reduced distraction tolerance) while insufficient load leaves the user vulnerable to missing relevant information; the 3–5 item sweet spot minimizes cognitive strain while maintaining focus.

concepts.definition: Wickens's framework showing that workload depends not only on task difficulty but on competition for specific resource pools (visual, auditory, cognitive, motor); performance degrades when simultaneous tasks compete for the same resource type.
key_refs: Wickens 2008 / Multiple Resources and Mental Workload, Ergonomics 51(5):584-595
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should exploit resource separation: pair visual graph navigation with verbal annotations, or alternate between visual search and motor interaction, to reduce competition on the same limited pool and effectively increase perceived capacity.

concepts.definition: Automatic, accurate enumeration of 3–4 objects without counting; accuracy breaks down beyond this range due to reliance on visuospatial working memory. Reflects the core capacity limit in visual object tracking.
key_refs: Trick & Pylyshyn 1994 / Why Are Variants of Visual Search Asymmetric?
Kaufman et al. 1949 / The Discrimination of Visual Number
concepts.implication: Counting or tracking visible nodes/controls in MetroGraph becomes effortful and error-prone beyond ~4 items; this directly maps to the hard bound on simultaneously manageable elements in a graph visualization.

concepts.definition: Failure to detect changes in a visual display when those changes occur during a saccade, blink, or visual interruption; reveals limits on distributed attention and transient working memory for changes not in focal attention.
key_refs: Simons & Rensink 2005 / Change Blindness: Past, Present, and Future, Trends in Cognitive Sciences 9(1):16-20
concepts.implication: Animated or gradual transitions in MetroGraph reduce change blindness risk; sudden or large updates outside the focal area may be missed, requiring explicit feedback mechanisms and reduced information density to ensure critical changes are perceived.

concepts.definition: Failure to notice unexpected objects or events in the visual field when attention is focused elsewhere, even when the stimulus is in clear view; demonstrates selective attention allocation limits.
key_refs: Mack & Rock 1998 / Inattentional Blindness
Simons & Chabris 1999 / Gorilla Experiment
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must make critical UI elements salient (notifications, alerts, key results) to overcome inattentional blindness; relying on subtle visual cues in a dense graph risks critical information being completely unnoticed.

concepts.definition: Scaife & Rogers's principle that well-designed external representations (diagrams, visualizations, written displays) reduce the working memory burden by externalizing information and allowing spatial/temporal constraint to guide reasoning.
key_refs: Scaife & Rogers 1996 / External Cognition: How Do Graphical Representations Work?, International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 45:185-213
Norman 1993 / Things That Make Us Smart
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's core value is externalizing database relationships as a visual graph, offloading working memory by allowing spatial and visual relationships to replace mental holding of abstract connections; effective design maximizes this offloading via clear layout and visual hierarchy.

concepts.definition: Pirolli & Card's functional model of analytical sensemaking as iterative cycles of information foraging (search, gather, filter) and synthesis (integrate, model, represent); external information architecture reduces working memory burden across iteration.
key_refs: Pirolli & Card 2005 / A Functional Model of Sensemaking in a Neurocognitive Architecture, International Journal of Human-Computer Studies 65(6):415-419
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should support fast foraging-synthesis loops: visual exploration and filtering keep working memory focused on the current analysis state, then explicit save/represent actions (e.g., node selection, subgraph snapshots) externalize intermediate conclusions to free capacity for the next cycle.

concepts.definition: Empirical finding that information exceeding working memory capacity degrades decision accuracy by 22–28%; visible information density beyond ~3–5 items actively harms task performance rather than merely failing to improve it.
key_refs: Speier et al. 1999 / The Impact of Time Pressure on Judgment and Decision Quality
2016 SIGHCI Study / InfoVis: The Impact of Information Overload on Decision Making Outcome in High Complexity Settings
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's value proposition includes reducing information overload harm: by carefully limiting visible elements and using progressive disclosure, it avoids the 22–28% performance degradation that unconstrained graph display causes in complex analytical tasks.

concepts.definition: Empirical evidence showing context switching between tasks incurs ~23 minute re-engagement time and causes working memory overload via concurrent task loading; resumption lag and attentional recalibration require substantial recovery.
key_refs: Iqbal & Bailey 2008 / Effects of Interruptions on Task Performance, Frustration, and Cognitive Workload
2024 PMC Study / Examining the Cognitive Processes Underlying Resumption Costs in Task-Interruption Contexts
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should minimize context switches between graph exploration and external tools/documentation; integrated analysis environment keeps working memory focused on the domain model, avoiding the 23-minute recovery cost when switching to chat, terminal, or other apps.

concepts.definition: Munzner's comprehensive framework for visualization design analyzing idioms (graphical encodings) against perceptual and cognitive constraints, including working memory and attention limits in mark-channel encoding.
key_refs: Munzner 2014 / Visualization Analysis & Design, CRC Press (2500+ citations)
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's visual encoding (node-link diagram) must be evaluated against Munzner's framework to ensure mark-channel choices (color, size, position, shape) respect working memory limits; effective encodings reduce the cognitive burden of interpretation.

concepts.definition: Tufte's principles for effective visualization establishing that cognitive effectiveness depends on minimizing visual noise, maximizing data-ink ratio, and respecting perceptual grouping; design within human perceptual and memory constraints.
key_refs: Tufte 1983 / The Visual Display of Quantitative Information
Tufte 1990 / Envisioning Information
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should apply Tufte's principles to graph visualization: every visible node or edge should carry necessary information; decorative or redundant elements waste the scarce resource of working memory attention.

concepts.definition: UI design pattern introduced by Nielsen (1995) revealing information gradually rather than all at once; directly addresses working memory constraints by reducing simultaneous visible controls and allowing staged cognitive processing.
key_refs: Nielsen 1995 / Progressive Disclosure
IxDF / Progressive Disclosure in UX Design
concepts.implication: Progressive disclosure is a primary design pattern for MetroGraph: filters, advanced options, and drill-down functionality should be hidden until needed, keeping the initial visible control count at or below 3–5 core items.

concepts.definition: Nielsen & Norman foundational heuristic: system feedback and visible state must be continuous and immediate, derived from working memory limitations requiring constant reinforcement and recognition (not recall) of system status.
key_refs: Nielsen & Norman 1994 / 10 Usability Heuristics for User Interface Design
NN/g Article / Visibility of System Status
concepts.implication: MetroGraph must maintain visible, real-time feedback of query state, filter status, and navigation context; relying on user recall of previous states exceeds working memory capacity and causes navigation errors.

concepts.definition: Nielsen's finding that spatial/visual location of UI elements is remembered better than labels or text; users navigate via spatial memory (where things are) rather than linguistic recall (what things are called).
key_refs: Nielsen & Norman 1994 / NN/g Article / Spatial Memory: Why It Matters for UX Design
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's interface should use consistent spatial locations for critical controls (toolbar position, legend placement, filter sidebar); this reduces working memory load by leveraging spatial memory, making the interface feel familiar and reducing navigation uncertainty.

concepts.definition: Early 20th-century perceptual grouping laws (proximity, similarity, closure, continuance) showing how the brain minimizes working memory load via automatic pattern recognition and figure-ground segregation.
key_refs: Wertheimer 1923 / Untersuchungen zur Lehre von der Gestalt
Gestalt Psychology principles
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's visual design should apply Gestalt principles to automatically organize nodes and edges into meaningful groups; proximity and similarity can reduce the effective count of distinct items users must hold in working memory.

concepts.definition: Kahneman & Tversky's framework distinguishing fast, intuitive System 1 thinking from slow, deliberate System 2 thinking; working memory limitations force reliance on System 1 heuristics under high cognitive load, increasing bias and error.
key_refs: Kahneman & Tversky 1974 / Judgment Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases, Science
Kahneman 2011 / Thinking, Fast and Slow
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should design for System 1 cognition at the working memory boundary: clear visual affordances, intuitive interactions, and reduced control density allow fast, accurate decisions; overload pushes users to unreliable heuristics and increases analytical errors.

concepts.definition: Empirical measure of UI cognitive load based on element count, spatial distribution, and visual clutter; recent studies establish direct correlation between visible control density and working memory demands in mobile and web interfaces.
key_refs: 2024 MDPI Study / A Measurement Model for Visual Complexity in HCI: Focusing on Visual Elements in Mobile GUI Design, Electronics 14(5):942
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should quantify visual complexity of the graph display (node count, edge density, visual clutter) and maintain it below thresholds documented in the literature; high visual complexity directly impairs working memory performance in graph comprehension tasks.

concepts.definition: Empirical comparison showing node-link diagrams are intuitive for sparse graphs but demand high working memory for dense connectivity tracking, while adjacency matrices scale better but require more abstract interpretation.
key_refs: Ghoniem, Fekete & Castagliola 2005 / Matrices or Node-Link Diagrams: Which Visual Representation is Better for Visualising Connectivity Models?, Information Visualization 5:1-13
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's choice of node-link encoding is appropriate for databases with moderate connectivity; for dense or very large graphs, hybrid or matrix views should be available to manage working memory demands as edge count increases.

concepts.definition: Survey evidence documenting empirical cognitive thresholds in graph visualization comprehension: node count, edge crossing, and visual density all degrade performance; effective working memory management requires limiting simultaneous visible items.
key_refs: A Survey of Empirical Studies on Graph Visualisation / Exploring the Limits of Complexity, ScienceDirect 2018
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's design should respect documented graph visualization limits: aim for <20 visible nodes in initial views, minimize edge crossings, and use filtering/progressive revelation for larger datasets; these directly map to working memory constraints.

concepts.concept: Visual Search Guided by Working Memory
concepts.definition: Working memory content actively guides attention during visual search via feature matching; search efficiency depends on working memory holding task-relevant features, which competes with processing visual information.
key_refs: Soto & Humphreys 2016 / Visual Working Memory Simultaneously Guides Facilitation and Inhibition During Visual Search, Attention, Perception, & Psychophysics
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's search and filter features should support explicit query formulation (keeping search criteria in working memory) and visual highlighting of matching results; reducing the user's need to mentally track search targets improves performance.

concepts.definition: Practitioner observation that 30–50% of software features provide marginal value; feature bloat increases UI control density directly beyond working memory capacity thresholds, reducing usability and causing 'surface-area bloat' (core wedge issue).
key_refs: 2024 QAT Industry Analysis / Feature Creep in Software Development – Avoid Common Pitfalls
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's design must resist feature creep: every visible control, button, and menu item consumes scarce working memory capacity; the wedge's core problem (RAG/agent-builder UI bloat) is fundamentally a feature-creep issue exacerbated by ignoring capacity limits.

concepts.concept: The Keyhole Effect (Chat Interfaces vs. Simultaneous Visibility)
concepts.definition: Contemporary finding (arXiv 2602) that sequential chat interfaces (one control visible at a time) fail at data analysis vs. simultaneous visibility; the 'keyhole' one-message-at-a-time paradigm trades control visibility for information density in the worst possible way.
key_refs: Bubble/MIT 2026 / The Keyhole Effect: Why Chat Interfaces Fail at Data Analysis, arXiv:2602.00947
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's core value is solving the keyhole effect: by showing multiple nodes, edges, and controls simultaneously (within working memory limits), it avoids the sequential bottleneck of chat-only interfaces while remaining cognitively manageable.

concepts.concept: Cognitive Divergence: LLM Context Windows vs. Human Working Memory
concepts.definition: Emerging divergence between LLM context window growth (100K+ tokens) and human working memory capacity (3–5 items); creates delegation feedback loop where AI-delegation patterns train users to expect information beyond their cognitive capacity.
key_refs: Bubble/MIT 2026 / The Cognitive Divergence: AI Context Windows, Human Attention Decline, and the Delegation Feedback Loop, arXiv:2603.26707
concepts.implication: MetroGraph addresses cognitive divergence by providing a UI that respects human working memory while leveraging LLM context for backend analysis; the visualization layer acts as a cognitive stabilizer, preventing attention decline from AI-UI mismatch.

concepts.concept: LLM Context Window as Working Memory Analogy
concepts.definition: Contemporary analytical framing (2026) treating LLM context windows as functional analogues to human working memory; both have hard capacity limits, both require management of information flow, and both degrade performance when overloaded.
key_refs: Atlan 2026 / Working Memory in LLMs: Context Window Deep Dive
Baddeley & Hitch 1974 / Working Memory Model (theoretical foundation)
concepts.implication: MetroGraph can bridge human-AI cognitive systems by treating both as capacity-limited: the visualization externally represents relationships that LLMs process internally, and the interface helps users manage their own working memory within the limits that systems they collaborate with impose.

concepts.definition: Emerging focus in RAG system design (GROUSER framework) on UI as key component for managing cognitive load across retrieval, synthesis, and user interaction; recognizes that information abundance without UI guidance exceeds user working memory.
key_refs: Mao et al. 2506 / RAG+: Enhancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Application-Aware Reasoning, arXiv:2506.11555
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's design for RAG contexts should actively manage cognitive load: retrieved information should be visualized with progressive disclosure, filtering, and hierarchical organization to keep working memory load within 3–5 items per decision point.

concepts.definition: Recent computational approaches (arXiv 2512) proposing objective measures of visualization complexity via visual feature analysis (element count, color, text, spatial distribution); aims to predict subjective cognitive load from objective visual properties.
key_refs: Bubble/MIT 2512 / Eye of the Beholder: Towards Measuring Visualization Complexity, arXiv:2512.05536
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should employ complexity metrics (node count, edge density, text labels, color variation) as design targets; maintaining metrics below empirically-derived thresholds ensures visualizations stay within working memory bounds.

concepts.concept: Information Visualization with Working Memory Metrics
concepts.definition: Established practice of evaluating visualization effectiveness using working memory metrics; shows quantifiable relationship between verbal and visual working memory capacity and chart type preference.
key_refs: OSTI 1110579 / Evaluating Information Visualizations with Working Memory Metrics
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's effectiveness should be evaluated against working memory metrics: time to comprehension, error rate in node/edge relationships, and cognitive effort should all reflect the optimization for 3–5 item capacity.

concepts.definition: Comprehensive survey of perception research in visualization documenting perceptual and cognitive capacity constraints including working memory limits on task performance; establishes empirical task-performance thresholds.
key_refs: 2021 arXiv Survey / A Survey of Perception-Based Visualization Studies by Task, arXiv:2107.07477
concepts.implication: MetroGraph design decisions (color, shape, spatial layout) should be grounded in the perception literature; documented task-performance thresholds provide quantitative targets for control density and visual encoding complexity.

concepts.definition: Bartlett & Rumelhart's framework showing that working memory interacts with long-term memory schemas; chunking via prior knowledge structures reduces memory load, but novel domains require explicit schema scaffolding.
key_refs: Rumelhart 1980 / Schemata: The Building Blocks of Cognition
Bartlett 1932 / Remembering: A Study in Experimental and Social Psychology
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should support schema formation for domain-specific structures (e.g., SQL table hierarchies, knowledge graph ontologies); visual patterns that align with user mental models reduce effective working memory load via chunking.

concepts.definition: UI design principle requiring interfaces to align with user's cognitive mental model (internal representation of system behavior); misalignment between interface and mental model increases working memory burden as users maintain dual models.
key_refs: Norman 1988 / The Design of Everyday Things
ScienceDirect / User Mental Models in Interface Design
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's interface should minimize the gap between the actual database model and the user's mental model; direct visual representation of table relationships and data dependencies leverages alignment to reduce working memory load.

concepts.definition: Research on stimulus salience showing that visually salient features (color contrast, motion, size, flicker) capture attention independently of task goals; can override working memory-guided visual search.
key_refs: Journal of Vision 2014 / Saliency, Attention, and Visual Search: An Information Theoretic Approach
concepts.implication: MetroGraph should carefully manage visual salience: critical nodes/edges should be salient (color, size), but decorative salience should be minimal; unconstrained salience competes with working memory-guided analysis and causes distraction.

concepts.definition: PLOS ONE evidence for a capacity-limited bottleneck in visual attention independent of stimulus encoding and retrieval; limits simultaneous processing of multiple information sets regardless of their perceptual separability.
key_refs: PLOS ONE 2014 / A Bottleneck Model of Set-Specific Capture, PLoS ONE 9(1):e88313
concepts.implication: Even perceptually distinct graph elements (different colors, sizes) face an attentional bottleneck when their count exceeds ~3–5 items; visual separation alone cannot overcome fundamental capacity limits, requiring interaction design to manage attention.

concepts.concept: Cognitive Load in Web Interface Design
concepts.definition: Empirical study establishing quantifiable relationship between visual complexity (element density, spatial distribution) and task difficulty on working memory demands in web interfaces; provides measurement framework for control density.
key_refs: ResearchGate 2024 / Cognitive Load in Web Interface Design: A Study Based on Visual Complexity and Task Difficulty
concepts.implication: MetroGraph's control density should be benchmarked against web interface standards; visual complexity measurement (element count, layout density) provides objective targets for progressive disclosure thresholds.
